title: Bonfire Night
when_text: 5 November (Lewes moves to the 4th when the 5th is a Sunday)
intro: On 5 November 1605 Guy Fawkes was caught beneath the House of Lords with 36 barrels of gunpowder, and Londoners lit bonfires for the king's escape. An act of Parliament made the day a thanksgiving, and for centuries it was a Protestant festival of sermons, bells and effigies. Its places run from Fawkes's York to the Midlands houses where the plot was hatched and ended, and to Lewes and Ottery St Mary, where it is kept most fiercely.

facts.title: Found in the undercroft
facts.text: A group of English Catholics planned to blow up King James I at the State Opening of Parliament. Late on 4 November 1605 a search party found Guy Fawkes, who gave his name as John Johnson, guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder in a rented undercroft directly beneath the House of Lords.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: During a search of the House of Lords on the evening of 4 November, Fawkes was discovered guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He was arrested, whereupon he gave his name as John Johnson.

facts.title: The letter to Lord Monteagle
facts.text: The plot was given away by an anonymous letter delivered to the Catholic peer Lord Monteagle on 26 October 1605, warning him to stay away from Parliament. He took it straight to Robert Cecil at Whitehall. Catesby suspected the newest recruit, Francis Tresham, who denied writing it.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On 26 October 1605, an anonymous letter of warning was sent to William Parker, 4th Baron Monteagle, a Catholic member of Parliament, who immediately showed it to the authorities.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Catesby, who had been due to go hunting with the King, suspected that Tresham was responsible for the letter

facts.title: The first bonfires
facts.text: Londoners lit bonfires to celebrate the king's escape, and in January 1606 Parliament passed the Observance of 5th November Act, which ordered a thanksgiving service in every church each 5 November. The act stayed on the statute book until 1859.

sources.title: Guy Fawkes Night (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Celebrating that the king had survived, people lit bonfires around London.

sources.title: Observance of 5th November Act 1605 (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The act remained on the statute book until 1859.

facts.title: Burning the pope, then the guy
facts.text: The first report of effigies burnt on 5 November is from 1625, when the pope and the devil went on the fire after Charles I married a Catholic princess. Effigies of Fawkes himself, carried round by children begging pennies, came at the end of the 18th century, and the day became Guy Fawkes Day.

sources.title: Guy Fawkes Night (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: on 5 November that year, effigies of the pope and the devil were burnt, the earliest such report of this practice

sources.title: Guy Fawkes Night (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Towards the end of the 18th century children began begging for money with effigies of Guy Fawkes and 5 November gradually became known as Guy Fawkes Day.

facts.title: Searching the cellars
facts.text: Before every State Opening of Parliament the Yeomen of the Guard search the cellars of the Palace of Westminster, a custom kept up since the plot. Their reward is a small glass of port.

sources.title: State Opening of Parliament (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: First, the cellars of the Palace of Westminster are searched by the Yeomen of the Guard.

sources.title: State Opening of Parliament (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Yeomen are paid for their services with a small glass of port wine

facts.title: A York childhood
facts.text: Guy Fawkes was born in Stonegate, York, in 1570 and baptised on 16 April at St Michael le Belfrey, opposite the Minster. He went to St Peter's School, as did the plotters John and Christopher Wright.

sources.title: Guy Fawkes (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Guy Fawkes was born in 1570 in Stonegate, York.

sources.title: St Michael le Belfrey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The church is famous for being the place where Guy Fawkes was baptised on 16 April 1570.

facts.title: The school that will not burn a guy
facts.text: St Peter's School in York, which claims a foundation in 627, has a bonfire and fireworks on 5 November but does not burn a guy, because Fawkes was an Old Peterite.

sources.title: St Peter's School, York (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: on Guy Fawkes Night, the school does not partake in the common tradition of burning a 'Guy' on the bonfire, as Guy Fawkes was an Old Peterite (alumnus).

facts.title: Fawkes's lantern
facts.text: The lantern Fawkes was carrying when he was arrested survives and is in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He was carrying a lantern now held in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford

sources.title: Ashmolean Museum (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The lantern that Gunpowder Plot conspirator Guy Fawkes carried in 1605

facts.title: Planning in the gatehouse
facts.text: Robert Catesby's family home at Ashby St Ledgers in Northamptonshire is said to have been the plotters' base: they met in the room over the gatehouse, out of sight of the main house. The fugitives stopped there on the evening of 5 November.

sources.title: Ashby St Ledgers (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the room above the Gatehouse, with its privacy from the main house and clear view of the surrounding area, Robert Catesby, his servant Thomas Bates and the other conspirators are said to have planned a great deal of the Gunpowder Plot.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The group of six conspirators stopped at Ashby St Ledgers at about 6 pm

facts.title: Last stand at Holbeche House
facts.text: The fleeing plotters reached Holbeche House in Staffordshire on 7 November. They laid out their rain-soaked gunpowder to dry before the fire, a spark set it off and several were burnt. Next morning the Sheriff of Worcestershire's men stormed the house and Catesby was killed.

sources.title: Holbeche House (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: several were maimed when gunpowder left to dry in front of the fire was ignited

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Richard Walsh (Sheriff of Worcestershire) and his company of 200 men besieged Holbeche House on the morning of 8 November.

facts.title: Hanged opposite Parliament
facts.text: Convicted at their trial on 27 January 1606, Fawkes, Thomas Wintour, Ambrose Rookwood and Robert Keyes were hanged, drawn and quartered a few days later in Old Palace Yard, opposite the building they had meant to destroy.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At their trial on 27 January 1606, eight of the surviving conspirators, including Fawkes, were convicted

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: were hanged, drawn and quartered, opposite the building they had planned to blow up, in the Old Palace Yard at Westminster

facts.title: Lewes, the bonfire capital
facts.text: Lewes in Sussex has held some of England's wildest 5 November celebrations since 1679. Its bonfire societies also remember the seventeen Protestant martyrs burnt in the town under Mary I, with seventeen burning crosses carried through the streets and a flaming tar barrel thrown into the River Ouse.

sources.title: Guy Fawkes Night (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: since 1679 Lewes has been the setting of some of England's most extravagant 5 November celebrations

sources.title: Lewes Bonfire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: To mark the demise of the 17 Lewes Martyrs, 17 burning crosses are carried through the town

facts.title: Tar barrels at Ottery St Mary
facts.text: In Ottery St Mary, Devon, people run through the streets carrying blazing barrels soaked in tar, a custom going back to the 17th century and held around Guy Fawkes Night.

sources.title: Ottery St Mary (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The town typically stages annual events around Guy Fawkes Night when, in a tradition dating from the 17th century, barrels soaked in tar are set alight, and carried aloft through parts of the town by residents

facts.title: Kept differently across the isles
facts.text: Bonfire Night spread through Britain and to the colonies. In Scotland bonfires are still lit in several cities; in Ireland it was overshadowed by William III's birthday and became sectarian from the 19th century and its celebration in Northern Ireland remains contentious.

sources.title: Guy Fawkes Night (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: (Its celebration in Northern Ireland remains controversial, unlike in Scotland where bonfires continue to be lit in various cities.)

places.name: Palace of Westminster
places.why: The target of the plot: the gunpowder lay in an undercroft beneath the House of Lords, and the cellars are still searched before each State Opening.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the undercroft directly beneath the House of Lords—the room where the plotters eventually stored the gunpowder

sources.title: State Opening of Parliament (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Since that year, the cellars have been searched, now largely, but not only, for ceremonial purposes.

places.name: Old Palace Yard, Westminster
places.why: Where Fawkes and three others were executed in January 1606.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: in the Old Palace Yard at Westminster

sources.title: St Michael le Belfrey (Wikipedia)

sources.quote: The present church building was built between 1525 and 1537

sources.title: St Michael le Belfrey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

sources.title: St Peter's School, York (Wikipedia)

sources.title: Ashmolean Museum (Wikipedia)

places.name: Ashby St Ledgers Manor House
places.why: The Catesbys' manor, said to be where much of the plot was planned, in the room over the gatehouse.

sources.title: Ashby St Ledgers (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Manor House is famous for being a location for the planning of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605.

places.name: Huddington Court
places.why: The moated Worcestershire home of the Wintour brothers, with two priest holes; the plot was partly hatched here and the fugitives sheltered here on 6 November. It is a private house.

sources.title: Huddington Court (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The plans of the Gunpowder Plot to blow up the Houses of Parliament in 1605 were, partially, conceived in Huddington Court.

sources.title: Huddington Court (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Following the arrest of Guy Fawkes the plotters fled to Huddington Court

places.name: Coughton Court
places.why: The Throckmortons' Tudor gatehouse house in Warwickshire, rented by the plotter Everard Digby; Thomas Bates rode here with news of the failure for the Jesuit priests.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Digby was asked by Catesby to rent Coughton Court near Alcester.

sources.title: Gunpowder Plot (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Bates left the group and travelled to Coughton Court to deliver a letter from Catesby, to Garnet and the other priests

places.name: Holbeche House
places.why: Where the plotters made their last stand on 8 November 1605.

sources.title: Holbeche House (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Some members of the Gunpowder Plot were either killed or captured at Holbeche House in 1605.

places.name: Lewes War Memorial
places.why: The centre of Lewes Bonfire night, where a wreath is laid during the processions.

sources.title: Lewes Bonfire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a wreath-laying ceremony occurs at the War Memorial in the centre of town
